claim: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep is characterized by slow-wave electrophysiological activity.
source: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, characterized by slow-wave electrophysiological activity, underlies several critical functions, including learning and memory.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing a defining characteristic of NREM sleep.

claim: NREM sleep underlies several critical functions, including learning and memory.
source: Non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, characterized by slow-wave electrophysiological activity, underlies several critical functions, including learning and memory.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction referencing established literature on sleep functions.

claim: NREM sleep is heterogeneous, varying in duration, depth, and spatially across the cortex.
source: However, NREM sleep is heterogeneous, varying in duration, depth, and spatially across the cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Astrocytic Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCR signaling separately control NREM sleep depth and duration, respectively.
source: We find that astrocytic Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCR signaling separately control NREM sleep depth and duration, respectively, and that astrocytic signaling causes differential changes in local and remote cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from DREADD manipulations.

claim: Astrocytic signaling causes differential changes in local and remote cortex.
source: We find that astrocytic Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCR signaling separately control NREM sleep depth and duration, respectively, and that astrocytic signaling causes differential changes in local and remote cortex.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data showing different effects in V1 versus contralateral frontal cortex.

claim: NREM sleep depth and duration can be independently controlled.
source: Past work has demonstrated that NREM sleep duration and depth can be independently controlled (Dijk and Beersma, 1989; Patrick and Gilbert, 1896).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sleep duration is mediated by subcortical nuclei that receive direct input from circadian centers and drive sleep/wake transitions through release of neuromodulatory signals.
source: sleep duration is mediated by subcortical nuclei that receive direct input from circadian centers and drive sleep/wake transitions through release of neuromodulatory signals (Holst and Landolt, 2018; Saper and Fuller, 2017; Lee and Dan, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: SWA intensity is largely regulated by cortical and thalamocortical circuits.
source: On the other hand, SWA intensity is largely regulated by cortical and thalamocortical circuits (Chen et al., 2012; Steriade et al., 1993; Lemieux et al., 2015; Volgushev et al., 2006; Steriade and Timofeev, 2003; Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014; Amzica and Steriade, 1995; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical calcium (Ca2+) signaling can act on a millisecond time-scale to modulate cortical synchrony during SWA while also engaging longer term signaling cascades that regulate the sleep/wake cycle.
source: For example, cortical calcium (Ca2+) signaling can act on a millisecond time-scale to modulate cortical synchrony during SWA while also engaging longer term signaling cascades that regulate the sleep/wake cycle (Ode et al., 2017; Tatsuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Astrocytes tile the cortex and can participate in bidirectional communication with thousands of neurons.
source: Astrocytes tile the cortex, can participate in bidirectional communication with thousands of neurons (Halassa et al., 2007; Allen and Barres, 2005; Bushong et al., 2002; Bazargani and Attwell, 2016), exhibit morphological and transcriptional changes during sleep (Bellesi et al., 2015), and regulate SWA under anesthesia (Szabó et al., 2017; Poskanzer and Yuste, 2016; Durkee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Astrocytes exhibit morphological and transcriptional changes during sleep.
source: Astrocytes tile the cortex, can participate in bidirectional communication with thousands of neurons (Halassa et al., 2007; Allen and Barres, 2005; Bushong et al., 2002; Bazargani and Attwell, 2016), exhibit morphological and transcriptional changes during sleep (Bellesi et al., 2015), and regulate SWA under anesthesia (Szabó et al., 2017; Poskanzer and Yuste, 2016; Durkee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bellesi et al., 2015.

claim: Astrocytes regulate SWA under anesthesia.
source: Astrocytes tile the cortex, can participate in bidirectional communication with thousands of neurons (Halassa et al., 2007; Allen and Barres, 2005; Bushong et al., 2002; Bazargani and Attwell, 2016), exhibit morphological and transcriptional changes during sleep (Bellesi et al., 2015), and regulate SWA under anesthesia (Szabó et al., 2017; Poskanzer and Yuste, 2016; Durkee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The majority of astrocyte Ca2+ activity is thought to result from upstream activation of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: The majority of astrocyte Ca2+ activity is thought to result from upstream activation of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Durkee et al., 2019; Di Castro et al., 2011; Agulhon et al., 2008; Kofuji and Araque, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Many astrocytic GPCRs are activated by neuromodulators, including those associated with sleep/wake regulation, such as norepinephrine, acetylcholine, and histamine.
source: Importantly, many astrocytic GPCRs are activated by neuromodulators, including those associated with sleep/wake regulation, such as norepinephrine, acetylcholine, and histamine.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about astrocytic receptors and neuromodulators.

claim: Both Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCRs activate IP3R2s and lead to increases in intracellular Ca2+ in astrocytes.
source: In astrocytes, both Gi- and Gq-coupled GPCRs activate IP3R2s and lead to increases in intracellular Ca2+ (Durkee et al., 2019; Mariotti et al., 2016; Nagai et al., 2019), while also engaging separate signaling cascades.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Endogenous Ca2+ activity is inversely correlated with SWA.
source: We find that endogenous Ca2+ activity is inversely correlated with SWA and exhibits bidirectional changes prior to sleep-wake transitions.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Endogenous Ca2+ activity exhibits bidirectional changes prior to sleep-wake transitions.
source: We find that endogenous Ca2+ activity is inversely correlated with SWA and exhibits bidirectional changes prior to sleep-wake transitions.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Astrocytic Gi-induced Ca2+ is sufficient to increase SWA (sleep depth).
source: astrocytic Gi-induced Ca2+ is sufficient to increase SWA (sleep depth), while sleep-wake transitions (sleep duration) is dependent on Gq-GPCRs.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from Gi-DREADD activation shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Sleep-wake transitions (sleep duration) is dependent on Gq-GPCRs.
source: astrocytic Gi-induced Ca2+ is sufficient to increase SWA (sleep depth), while sleep-wake transitions (sleep duration) is dependent on Gq-GPCRs.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from Gq-DREADD activation shown in Figure 6.

claim: Manipulating astrocytic Ca2+ in primary visual cortex (V1) alters not only local SWA, but also affects SWA in contralateral frontal cortex (FC).
source: We demonstrate a role for astrocytes in both local and cortex-wide sleep regulation; manipulating astrocytic Ca2+ in primary visual cortex (V1) alters not only local SWA, but also affects SWA in contralateral frontal cortex (FC).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Local changes in SWA arise from greater changes in delta waves.
source: Further, we find that while local changes in SWA arise from greater changes in delta waves, remote SWA effects in FC are due to increases in slow oscillations.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Remote SWA effects in FC are due to increases in slow oscillations.
source: Further, we find that while local changes in SWA arise from greater changes in delta waves, remote SWA effects in FC are due to increases in slow oscillations.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I-J.

claim: Ca2+ event rate and SWA are negatively correlated.
source: By dividing entire 2–3 hr recordings into two-min bins, we found that Ca2+ event rate and SWA were negatively correlated (Figure 1D), that is when SWA is low, astrocyte Ca2+ event rate is high, and vice versa.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis (Pearson's correlation, p<0.0005).

claim: Ca2+ event rate was highest during locomotory wake, lower during stationary wake, and lowest during sleep.
source: As predicted by the negative correlation between event rate and SWA (Figure 1D), we found that Ca2+ event rate was highest during locomotory wake, lower during stationary wake, and lowest during sleep (Figure 1F).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F with statistical analysis (rank sum test).

claim: SWA was highest during sleep, lower during stationary wake, and lowest during locomotory wake.
source: To confirm, we compared SWA in the three behavioral states and found an inverse relationship of Ca2+ event rate, namely SWA was highest during sleep, lower during stationary wake, and lowest during locomotory wake (Figure 1G).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis (rank sum test).

claim: Locomotory wake Ca2+ events were larger in size and duration than events observed in the other two states.
source: As predicted by the large, synchronous bursts observed during locomotion, we found locomotory wake Ca2+ events were larger in size and duration than events observed in the other two states.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with statistical analysis (rank sum test).

claim: When controlling for locomotion, there were no differences in size, duration, or amplitude of events between sleep and stationary wake when these features were compared individually.
source: However, when we controlled for locomotion we did not find differences in size, duration, or amplitude of events between sleep and stationary wake when these features were compared individually (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There are significant differences between sleep and stationary wake in all five principal components examined when multiple event features are incorporated.
source: While the largest differences in each PC were between locomotory wake and the other two states, we also found significant differences between sleep and stationary wake in all five PCs examined (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis (two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).

claim: There are unique spatial, temporal, and amplitude signatures of sleep-specific astrocyte Ca2+ events when multiple features are incorporated.
source: Together, this analysis demonstrates that while no state-specific differences are observed by comparisons of individual event features, there are unique spatial, temporal, and amplitude signatures of sleep-specific astrocyte Ca2+ events when multiple features are incorporated.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ca2+ frequency and SWA are negatively correlated within stationary behavioral states.
source: We next examined the relationship between astrocyte Ca2+ event frequency and SWA within stationary behavioral states and found, similar to Figure 1D, a negative correlation between Ca2+ frequency and SWA (Figure 1H).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H with statistical analysis (Pearson's correlation, p<0.0005).

claim: IP3R2 KO mice show a decreased correlation between Ca2+ event rate and SWA compared to controls.
source: In IP3R2 KO mice, Ca2+ event rate and SWA were negatively correlated, but the correlation was decreased compared to controls (Figure 1I), suggesting the astrocyte-SWA relationship is at least partially dependent on the IP3R2.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I with statistical analysis (Pearson's correlation).

claim: The change in correlation between control and IP3R2 KO was most dramatic in sleep, implicating IP3R2-dependent astrocytic Ca2+ signaling in the regulation of SWA intensity in the sleep state.
source: The change in correlation between control and IP3R2 KO was most dramatic in sleep, implicating IP3R2-dependent astrocytic Ca2+ signaling in the regulation of SWA intensity in the sleep state.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparison of correlations shown in Figure 1H and 1I.

claim: Ca2+ events were preceded by decreases in SWA and followed by increases in SWA during sleep and stationary wake.
source: We found a pattern in which Ca2+ events were preceded by decreases in SWA and followed by increases in SWA (Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SWA modulation around Ca2+ events was decreased in IP3R2 KO mice.
source: Further, this SWA modulation was decreased in IP3R2 KO mice (Figure 2C, right, Figure 2D), indicating partial dependence of this relationship on IP3R2s (as in Figure 1I).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C (right) and Figure 2D.

claim: Gi-DREADD activation in astrocytes increased Ca2+ event frequency across the entire 2 hr recording period after CNO administration.
source: Here, we confirmed that Gi-DREADD activation indeed altered astrocyte Ca2+, causing an increase in event frequency across the entire 2 hr recording period after CNO administration (Figure 3C–D, Video 2).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Activation of Gi-DREADDs by CNO significantly increased SWA during sleep compared to a saline injection in the same animal.
source: Next, we asked whether Gi-induced Ca2+ event increases were sufficient to alter SWA. We found that activation of Gi-DREADDs by CNO significantly increased SWA during sleep compared to a saline injection in the same animal (Figure 3E).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Total time spent in sleep and wake was not affected by Gi-DREADD activation.
source: In contrast, total time spent in sleep and wake was not affected by Gi-DREADD activation (Figure 3F,H).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3H with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Gi-GPCR activation did not change SWA during the entire wake state.
source: In contrast to the change in SWA during sleep (Figure 3E), we found no change in SWA during the entire wake state (Figure 3G).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: CNO administration did not significantly increase astrocyte Ca2+ in IP3R2 KO mice expressing Gi-DREADDs.
source: Unlike control mice (Figure 3C–D), CNO administration did not significantly increase astrocyte Ca2+ in IP3R2 KO mice (Figure 3I), demonstrating that Gi-DREADD-induced Ca2+ events rely, at least in part, on IP3R2.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: In IP3R2 KO mice, there was no significant change in SWA with CNO administration in Gi-DREADD experiments.
source: In accordance with the lack of change in Ca2+ in the IP3R2 KO animals, we also observed no significant change in SWA with CNO administration (Figure 3J), indicating that the change in sleep depth we observe (Figure 3E) is dependent on IP3R2.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Slow oscillations had larger positive peaks and larger positive-to-negative deflections that occurred within 500 ms.
source: Slow oscillations had larger positive peaks and larger positive-to-negative deflections that occurred within 500 ms (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Gi-DREADD activation did not change the rate of delta waves or slow oscillations during sleep.
source: We first looked at the effect of astrocytic Gi-DREADD activation on the number of identified delta waves and slow oscillations, and found no effect on the rate of delta waves or slow oscillations during sleep (Figure 4E).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: CNO administration resulted in higher peak and lower trough amplitudes for delta waves.
source: Indeed, by plotting peak vs. trough amplitude, we observed a clear change in delta waves after CNO, resulting in higher peak and lower trough amplitudes (Figure 4G).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There was a significant increase in peak-trough amplitude for delta waves after CNO administration.
source: Similarly, we quantified the change in total peak – trough amplitude after CNO administration. While we saw a significant increase in size for delta waves (Figure 4H) and slow oscillations (Figure 4K) compared to saline controls in the same animal, the change in delta waves was significantly higher than that for slow oscillations (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: The change in delta wave amplitude was significantly higher than that for slow oscillations after Gi-DREADD activation.
source: While we saw a significant increase in size for delta waves (Figure 4H) and slow oscillations (Figure 4K) compared to saline controls in the same animal, the change in delta waves was significantly higher than that for slow oscillations (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Astrocyte Ca2+, through Gi-GPCR signaling, preferentially increases SWA by altering delta wave amplitude.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that astrocyte Ca2+, through Gi-GPCR signaling, preferentially increases SWA by altering delta wave amplitude.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ca2+ events consistently increased before the sleep-to-wake transition and decreased before the wake-to-sleep transition.
source: We found a pattern in which Ca2+ events consistently increased before the sleep-to-wake transition and decreased before the wake-to-sleep transition (Figure 5A).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ca2+ event rate increased in the last third of sleep and decreased in the last third of wake.
source: In so doing, we found that Ca2+ event rate increased in the last third of sleep and decreased in the last third of wake (Figure 5D).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: The changes in event rate preceding transitions were abolished in IP3R2 KO mice.
source: As predicted, we found that the changes in event rate preceding transitions were abolished in IP3R2 KO mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IP3R2 KO mice did not exhibit the same increase in event rate in the last third of sleep as control mice.
source: When quantifying the change in event rate in the last third of sleep and wake for IP3R2 KO mice, we found that IP3R2 KO mice did not exhibit the same increase in event rate in the last third of sleep (Figure 5D, left).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D (left) with statistical analysis (unpaired t-test).

claim: Ca2+ dynamics only increased in the first 5–10 min after I.P. injection of CNO in Gq-DREADD experiments, after which Ca2+ dynamics were almost completely abolished.
source: However, we were surprised to find that Ca2+ dynamics only increased in the first 5–10 min after I.P. injection of CNO (150.9% ± 135.9, Video 3). After this initial period of increased Ca2+ events, Ca2+ dynamics were almost completely abolished (−97.3% ± 0.79%, Figure 6C–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H, Video 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D and Video 3.

claim: Mice spent significantly more time in sleep after CNO administration during the Ca2+ suppression period in Gq-DREADD experiments.
source: We found that mice spent significantly more time in sleep after CNO administration (Figure 6E, left).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E (left) with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: In the absence of Gq-GPCR-mediated Ca2+ events, mice made fewer sleep-to-wake transitions.
source: Further, in the absence of Gq-GPCR-mediated Ca2+ events, mice made fewer sleep-to-wake transitions (Figure 6F, left) and accordingly, we observed fewer sleep bouts of longer duration (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F (left) with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Astrocyte Ca2+ is important for both wake-to-sleep transitions and sleep-to-wake transitions.
source: However, we also observed less frequent transitions out of wake, demonstrating that astrocyte Ca2+ is important for both wake-to-sleep transitions (Figure 6F, right), and sleep-to-wake transitions (Figure 6F, left).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: During the initial period with elevated Ca2+ activity in Gq-DREADD experiments, there was a significant decrease in the percent time sleeping.
source: However, of the animals that exhibited some sleep in either the CNO or saline condition (n = 4), we observed a significant decrease in the percent time sleeping (Figure 6G).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Ca2+ suppression via Gq-GPCR manipulation had no significant effect on SWA during sleep.
source: In contrast to manipulation of the Gi-GPCRs, we found that Ca2+ suppression via Gq-GPCR manipulation had no significant effect on SWA during sleep (Figure 6H).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Astrocytic regulation of SWA is specifically dependent on the Gi-GPCR pathway.
source: This suggests that astrocytic regulation of SWA is specifically dependent on the Gi-GPCR pathway and provides further evidence that astrocytic Gi- and Gq-GPCR signaling regulate separable sleep/wake features.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the differential effects of Gi- and Gq-DREADD manipulations on SWA.

claim: SWA in FC decreased before and increased after V1 Ca2+ event onsets, although the magnitude of this modulation was smaller than that observed locally.
source: Using Ca2+ event-triggered averages, we found a similar relationship with V1 Ca2+ events and FC as previously described (Figure 2C): SWA in FC decreased before and increased after V1 Ca2+ event onsets, although the magnitude of this modulation was smaller than that observed locally (Figure 7C).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: V1-FC coherence (between 5 and 10 Hz) was higher immediately following astrocyte Ca2+ events when compared to coherence measured from randomly chosen epochs.
source: We found that the V1-FC coherence (between 5 and 10 Hz) was higher immediately following astrocyte Ca2+ events when compared to coherence measured from randomly chosen epochs (Figure 7D).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: There was an increase in astrocyte event-locked coherence (0–15 Hz) at the end of sleep periods, in the 15 s prior to sleep-to-wake transitions.
source: We also found an increase in astrocyte event-locked coherence (0–15 Hz) at the end of sleep periods, in the 15 s prior to sleep-to-wake transitions (Figure 7E).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E with statistical analysis (unpaired t-test).

claim: Increasing Ca2+ via Gi-DREADDs in V1 was sufficient to increase SWA in the contralateral frontal cortex, although this increase was smaller than that observed in V1.
source: Here, we found that increasing Ca2+ via Gi-DREADDs in V1 was sufficient to increase SWA in the contralateral frontal cortex, although this increase was smaller than that observed in V1 (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-H with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: The SWA change in FC was accounted for by a significant increase in slow oscillation amplitude, but not delta wave amplitude.
source: We also found that the SWA change was accounted for by a significant increase in slow oscillation amplitude, but not delta wave (Figure 7I; Figure 7J).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7I and 7J with statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: The change in slow oscillation amplitude in FC was similar to the change of the slow oscillation amplitude in V1.
source: Moreover, the change in slow oscillation amplitude in FC (Figure 7J, 6.8 ± 2.2%) was similar to the change of the slow oscillation amplitude in V1 (Figure 4L, 8.8 ± 3.2%), suggesting that slow oscillations generated in V1 travelled to FC.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of data from Figure 7J and Figure 4L.

claim: Astrocytes can influence cortex-wide dynamics on a large scale via specific changes to the slow oscillation component of SWA.
source: These results indicate that astrocytes can influence cortex-wide dynamics on a large scale via specific changes to the slow oscillation component of SWA.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cortical astrocytes regulate distinct features of sleep via differential GPCR signaling.
source: Using simultaneous 2P imaging of astrocyte Ca2+ and electrophysiology across wake and sleep, we have demonstrated that cortical astrocytes regulate distinct features of sleep via differential GPCR signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Astrocyte Ca2+ is sufficient to increase SWA during sleep through specific enhancement of delta waves, which is specific to Gi-, not Gq-, GPCR-induced Ca2+.
source: With chemogenetics, we demonstrated that astrocyte Ca2+ is sufficient to increase SWA during sleep through specific enhancement of delta waves. This is specific to Gi-, not Gq-, GPCR-induced Ca2+.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data from Gi- and Gq-DREADD manipulations.

claim: Gq-, but not Gi-, GPCR Ca2+ signaling is important for mediating sleep/wake transitions.
source: In contrast, Gq-, but not Gi-, GPCR Ca2+ signaling is important for mediating sleep/wake transitions.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data from Gi- and Gq-DREADD manipulations.

claim: Astrocyte Ca2+ has far-reaching, cortex-wide effects on SWA and slow oscillations.
source: Lastly, we demonstrated that astrocyte Ca2+ has far-reaching, cortex-wide effects on SWA and slow oscillations.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Following sleep deprivation, recovery sleep has higher sleep depth but the duration is not significantly changed.
source: Previous work has also shown separation in sleep depth and duration by demonstrating that following sleep deprivation, recovery sleep has higher sleep depth but the duration is not significantly changed (Dijk and Beersma, 1989; Patrick and Gilbert, 1896).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ca2+ has been suggested to mechanistically link the regulation of sleep duration and depth.
source: On the other hand, Ca2+ has been suggested to mechanistically link the regulation of sleep duration and depth (Ode et al., 2017; Tatsuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Astrocyte Ca2+ changes with circadian rhythm in the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
source: In fact, astrocyte Ca2+ changes with circadian rhythm in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (Brancaccio et al., 2017) and increases with sleep need after sleep deprivation (Ingiosi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Astrocyte Ca2+ increases with sleep need after sleep deprivation.
source: In fact, astrocyte Ca2+ changes with circadian rhythm in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (Brancaccio et al., 2017) and increases with sleep need after sleep deprivation (Ingiosi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ingiosi et al., 2020.

claim: Delta waves are thought to promote the weakening of memories, while slow oscillations support memory consolidation.
source: Delta waves are thought to promote the weakening of memories, while slow oscillations support memory consolidation (Genzel et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Delta waves are more local than slow oscillations and are thought to be generated within the cortex.
source: Delta waves are more local than slow oscillations and are thought to be generated within the cortex (Genzel et al., 2014; Siclari and Tononi, 2017; Siclari et al., 2014; Bernardi et al., 2018; Spoormaker et al., 2010; Nir et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DOWN states are thought to be generated through GABAergic inhibition.
source: Since our Gi-DREADD manipulation was restricted within the cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and DOWN states are thought to be generated through GABAergic inhibition (Chen et al., 2012; Lemieux et al., 2015; Sheroziya and Timofeev, 2014; Zucca et al., 2017), we hypothesize that Gi-GPCR signaling in astrocytes mediates the local synchronization of delta waves via control of inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Slow oscillations are more global than delta waves.
source: Slow oscillations are more global than delta waves.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: 1 mg/kg CNO did not alter Ca2+ dynamics or sleep features in the absence of DREADD expression.
source: Because of the known sedative effects of CNO, we first verified that CNO itself (1 mg/kg, I.P) did not alter Ca2+ dynamics or sleep features in the absence of DREADD expression. We found no change in Ca2+ dynamics or sleep features between administration of 1 mg/kg CNO and the saline control (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gi-DREADD activation in astrocytes is consistent with studies of astrocytic Ca2+ activity in ex vivo slices and in anesthetized mice.
source: This finding is consistent with studies of astrocytic Ca2+ activity in ex vivo slices and in anesthetized mice (Durkee et al., 2019; Nagai et al., 2019; Chai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Astrocytic Gq-DREADD activation in vivo has been performed previously.
source: Although astrocytic Gq-DREADD activation in vivo has been performed previously (Durkee et al., 2019; MacDonald et al., 2020; Bonder and McCarthy, 2014; Adamsky et al., 2018), validation of Gq-DREADD-mediated astrocytic Ca2+ increases has only been performed under anesthesia or ex vivo, in part because several in vivo astrocyte DREADD experiments have been carried out in brain regions that are less accessible than cortex (MacDonald et al., 2020; Adamsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Validation of Gq-DREADD-mediated astrocytic Ca2+ increases has only been performed under anesthesia or ex vivo.
source: Although astrocytic Gq-DREADD activation in vivo has been performed previously (Durkee et al., 2019; MacDonald et al., 2020; Bonder and McCarthy, 2014; Adamsky et al., 2018), validation of Gq-DREADD-mediated astrocytic Ca2+ increases has only been performed under anesthesia or ex vivo, in part because several in vivo astrocyte DREADD experiments have been carried out in brain regions that are less accessible than cortex (MacDonald et al., 2020; Adamsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gq-GPCR signaling canonically results in an increase in Ca2+ activity via IP3-dependent release of intracellular Ca2+.
source: Canonically, Gq-GPCR signaling results in an increase in Ca2+ activity via IP3-dependent release of intracellular Ca2+ (Petravicz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Petravicz et al., 2008.

claim: The observed inhibition of astrocyte Ca2+ after Gq-DREADD activation could be due to depletion of intracellular Ca2+ stores and/or interference with store-operated Ca2+ channels.
source: The observed inhibition of astrocyte Ca2+ could be due to depletion of intracellular Ca2+ stores and/or interference with store-operated Ca2+ channels (Sakuragi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Sakuragi et al., 2017.

claim: Fluorescence in both somas and processes remained elevated above baseline after 1 mg/kg CNO in Gq-DREADD experiments.
source: We found that fluorescence in both somas and processes remained elevated above baseline after 1 mg/kg CNO (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I), which suggests that Ca2+ levels may be clamped at saturating levels.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: A dramatic increase in Ca2+ activity was observed in response to the wake cocktail in ex vivo slices.
source: As predicted from previous studies reporting astrocytic Ca2+ increases to various neuromodulators (Ding et al., 2013; Khan et al., 2001; Takata et al., 2011; Shelton and McCarthy, 2000; Pankratov and Lalo, 2015), we observed a dramatic increase in Ca2+ activity in response to the cocktail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J and citations to previous studies.

claim: After the initial increase in Ca2+ in response to the wake cocktail, GCaMP fluorescence did not return to baseline levels, but remained high and further Ca2+ events were almost completely absent.
source: However, after this initial increase in Ca2+, GCaMP fluorescence did not return to baseline levels, but remained high and further Ca2+ events were almost completely absent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J), similar to in vivo dynamics observed 5–10 min after CNO administration.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: No further increase in astrocyte Ca2+ was observed in response to a second dose of wake cocktail in ex vivo slices.
source: In contrast to the initial Ca2+ increase, we observed no further increase in astrocyte Ca2+ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.
